title: Parity and odd/even structure
transcript: Parity tells us whether a whole number is odd or even. Think of an even number as pairs, and an odd number as pairs with one left over. Look for a move or arrangement that must preserve parity. One quick check can rule out a long search.

AMC practice may hide odd and even structure in jumps, paired objects, or a game where each move changes some pieces. A Rossmoyne style proof can use parity or a two-colour pattern to explain why a proposed arrangement is impossible.
Is the sum of fifteen and twenty odd or even? Try to decide by pairing. Think about how many unpaired counters each addend would have.

fifteen has one extra counter after pairing. twenty is fully paired, so it contributes no extra counter. The total has one extra and is odd. The exact sum is thirty-five, which confirms the pairing argument.
A counter starts at fifteen on a number line. Each move adds or subtracts an even number of steps. Can it ever reach twenty? The length and direction may change on each move.

Adding an even number is adding entire pairs. Subtracting an even number also removes entire pairs. Neither change affects the leftover one. The counter starts at odd fifteen, and every later position must remain odd. The target twenty is even, so it is unreachable.
A four by four square grid has its top left and bottom right corners removed. Can you cover every remaining square with dominoes, each covering two adjacent squares? No overlap is allowed.

Colour the grid like a chessboard. A domino always covers one square of each colour, because adjacent squares have opposite colours. The grid began with eight squares of each colour. The opposite corners in this even-sized grid have the same colour. Removing both corners gives six of one colour and eight of the other. Dominoes cannot balance these counts.

There are an even number of remaining cells, so a total cell count alone would allow a whole number of dominoes. The stronger test is the split by colouring. Rotating a domino does not change its need for one square of each colour.

Try a parity question before calculating a big total. Label each value odd or even and see how the labels combine. A matching parity does not prove that every move is allowed. Use a construction as well whenever the question asks what can be achieved.

Mark what one move does to parity. Decide whether the leftover changes, stays fixed, or follows a pattern. Check whether the target has the required parity or colour balance. Write one sentence explaining why every legal move obeys that rule.
